components.text: Scientific mechanisms can omit God without settling deeper explanatory or metaphysical questions.
Whether excluding God from ordinary scientific mechanisms also settles the deeper metaphysical question.
Mathematical and apparent design considerations do not by themselves warrant inference to God.
A design inference must address questions about the designer and defective features in creation.
Whether apparent rational design warrants an inference from mathematical order to God.
Whether invoking a divine mind resolves deeper explanatory questions rather than relocating them.
Christian faith is an evidence-based commitment rather than belief adopted independently of reasons.
Asking who created God misconstrues the biblical God as a created designer.
Whether Christian faith is a reasonless commitment rather than an evidence-based one.
Whether asking about the creator of God is a valid objection to the biblical conception of God.
Evidence can shape religious interpretation without establishing Christian belief by scientific-style inference.
Whether evidence supporting religious interpretation amounts to an inferential basis for Christian belief.
Nonlaboratory historical questions can be assessed through inference to the best explanation.
Christian commitment rests on cumulative intellectual, historical, experiential, and transformative evidence.
Whether Christian commitment can rest on nonlaboratory cumulative inference rather than proof.
Whether faith must precede and organize every purported item of evidence.
The religious significance of resurrection need not depend on proving a physical event.
The disciples' transformed conviction can carry the resurrection's spiritual meaning.
Whether resurrection significance requires establishing a physically real supernatural event.
A Gospel sign's physical occurrence can be integral to its disclosure of Jesus' identity.
Divine action may add an event without constituting a violation of natural law.
Whether Gospel meaning can dispense with the real occurrence of the narrated divine act.
Miracle narratives can be explained through transformative moral and communal action rather than supernatural intervention.
Whether supernatural physical occurrence is required for a Gospel miracle narrative's significance.
Theological meaning is strengthened when the Gospel narrative rests on an actual event.
Real signs progressively disclose Christ's identity and provide grounds for belief.
Whether Gospel meaning is strengthened by real signs rather than exhausted by a moral reinterpretation.
Whether religious significance can remain adequate when physical occurrence is treated as unimportant.
Whether Gospel miracle narratives require supernatural events rather than moral reinterpretation.
Whether Christian supernatural claims supply more than secular moral meaning when confronting suffering.
Whether physical resurrection has indispensable significance as a ground of hope.
A response to evil must address the severe cost that perpetrators' freedom imposes on innocent victims.
Resurrection hope does not by itself show that permitting such suffering evidences a good God.
Whether Christian hope and divine participation answer the evidential force of victims' severe suffering.
The pro account may interpret suffering through a prior conviction of divine love rather than infer goodness from suffering-related evidence.
Whether suffering independently evidences divine goodness or is interpreted through a prior Christian conviction.
Whether the claimed cumulative case genuinely produces belief rather than presupposing its theological framework.
Preventing all moral evil through determinism would remove the freedom required for genuinely chosen love.
The proposed justification appeals to the value of free persons and loving relationships rather than merely assuming divine goodness.
The argument must explain why freedom's value can justify the particular magnitude of harm suffered by victims.
Whether preventing moral evil would require eliminating the freedom necessary for love and human relationship.
Whether the free-will account supplies an independent explanatory consideration rather than only prior faith.
